title: Sensex Sheds 649 Points as Brent Touches $108 on New Middle East Flare-Ups
excerpt: India's equity benchmarks tumbled in early Friday trade after Brent crude surged toward $108 a barrel on fresh fighting in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, wiping out Thursday's tentative recovery and sealing a fifth straight weekly loss.
body:
• Indian benchmarks tumbled in early Friday trade — the Sensex fell 649 points and the Nifty lost 1% — after Brent crude surged toward $108 a barrel on escalating Middle East fighting.
  • Iran-aligned Houthi forces seized Yemen's port city of Mocha and advanced toward the Hanish islands, threatening Red Sea shipping, while tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to half its 10-day average.
  • The selloff erased Thursday's tentative 138-point recovery and set both indices on course for a fifth consecutive weekly loss; the rupee slid to its sharpest weekly drop since May.
  • Rising global bond yields compounded the pressure, with the US 10-year Treasury yield touching 4.98%, as investors priced in higher inflation ahead of the Federal Reserve's September 16 meeting.

Indian equity benchmarks opened sharply lower on Friday, September 11, as a fresh escalation of the Middle East conflict drove Brent crude toward $108 a barrel and sent investors rushing out of risk assets. The BSE Sensex was trading at 74,253.17 as of 9:41 AM IST, down 649.42 points or 0.87%, while the Nifty 50 dropped to 23,243.55, down 234.25 points or 1%, according to HDFC Sky data. Both indices hit intraday lows of around 74,160 and 23,231 respectively during the morning session.

The speed of the drop caught traders off guard. Thursday had ended on a mildly positive note — the Sensex rose 138.36 points to close at 74,902.59 and the Nifty gained 46.30 points to 23,477.80, with media and banking stocks leading the recovery. That rebound, in hindsight, lasted less than a full trading session.

Red Sea escalation jolts crude markets

The immediate trigger was a widening of the six-month-old Middle East war. Iran-aligned Houthi forces seized control of Yemen's port city of Mocha on Thursday and advanced down the Red Sea coast toward the strategic Hanish islands, gaining further leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the critical southern outlet of the Red Sea, military sources told Reuters. The advance came hours after US President Donald Trump said he expected the Iran war to end after the November US midterm elections, even as Iran's foreign ministry accused Washington of violating a ceasefire agreement through continued strikes on Iranian oil tankers.

Crude benchmarks reacted across the board. Brent crude traded up 0.2% at $107.9 on Friday morning, having climbed past $105 overnight. WTI crude edged up to $102.57 a barrel, while Murban crude surged 5.36% to $122.48 and the OPEC basket jumped 4.46% to $112.25. On the ground, the shipping picture is worsening: just seven vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, half the 10-day average, as fighting resumed and set back earlier progress in reopening the waterway. UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg warned the international community must act to address "a new and more dangerous phase" in the widening conflict.

A rough week gets rougher

Friday's decline caps a bruising stretch for Indian equities. Both the Nifty and Sensex have fallen about 2% this week and roughly 4.8% over the last five weeks, Reuters reported, putting them on track for a fifth consecutive weekly loss. The damage has been broad: fourteen of the 16 major sectors logged weekly losses. The Nifty IT index slumped 5.8% in its biggest weekly percentage drop since April, weighed down by the prospect of a Fed rate hike next week. Heavyweight financials lost 1.9% for the week — HDFC Bank fell for a sixth week in a row amid uncertainty over its CEO succession — and Reliance Industries, the Nifty's third-heaviest stock, dropped 4.9%.

On Friday morning, metal and realty stocks bore the brunt of the selling: Nifty Realty plunged 3.65% and Nifty Metal slid 2.82%. Hindalco Industries was the steepest Nifty decliner, falling 3.62%, followed by Tata Steel (-2.37%), JSW Steel (-2.11%), Bajaj Finance (-2.10%) and Shriram Finance (-2.09%). Among the few gainers, ONGC rose 1.92%, benefiting directly from elevated crude prices, with Tech Mahindra, Infosys and TCS also holding up.

"Such a sharp surge in Brent crude was not anticipated by the markets. Unless the Middle East crisis is resolved and Brent crude eases substantially, markets are in for a longer period of subdued performance."

— Ambareesh Baliga, independent market analyst, Mumbai

Pressure from three directions

Oil is not the only force weighing on equities. Foreign investors net sold Indian shares worth 4.38 billion rupees ($45.89 million) on Thursday, according to provisional data, and have offloaded $1.36 billion of shares so far in September. A busy IPO season — with large offerings from the National Stock Exchange of India and potentially from Mukesh Ambani-backed Jio Platforms — has also absorbed liquidity and weighed on secondary-market demand.

The third shock is rates. Rising oil prices inflamed inflation fears and sent global bond yields to multi-year highs; the US 10-year Treasury yield touched 4.98% on Friday. US markets closed lower across the board on Thursday — the Dow fell 316.56 points to 52,064.10, the S&P 500 dropped 0.58% and the Nasdaq declined 0.65% — as surging oil, a bond selloff and hotter-than-expected wholesale inflation data landed on the same day. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 tumbled 2.76% on Friday, while Shanghai, Hong Kong and Australia all traded sharply lower.

"The sharp increase in crude prices is likely to heighten concerns over India's import bill, inflation and corporate margins, keeping risk appetite subdued."

— Ponmudi R, CEO, Enrich Money

The currency is feeling it too. The Indian rupee weakened 1% this week, marking its sharpest weekly drop since mid-May, as importers rushed to buy dollars against the surging crude bill.

What to watch

Three catalysts now set the near-term direction. First, crude: as Hareesh V, Head of Commodity Research at Geojit Investments, noted, "the sustainability of crude oil above $100 per barrel will largely depend on how geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, particularly between the US and Iran, evolve in the coming weeks." Shipping data from Hormuz and the Red Sea will be the earliest signal of any de-escalation.

Second, the Federal Reserve's policy meeting on September 16. With US inflation running hot, traders are pricing in a hawkish outcome that would lift the dollar and drain more foreign capital from emerging markets — a scenario India's IT exporters would face with particular discomfort. Third, domestic flows: whether domestic institutional buyers keep absorbing the foreign selloff, as they did earlier this week, will determine if the 23,000 level on the Nifty holds.

For now, analysts counsel patience over bottom-fishing. Ruchit Thakur of VT Markets said that with Brent past $108, investors should stay cautious and favor defensive sectors — pharmaceuticals, healthcare, utilities and select IT exporters — while staggering purchases rather than trying to catch the exact bottom.
